props.description: Install, authenticate and configure Claude Code, Codex, Pi, OpenCode and GitHub Copilot for Archon.

text.insert: Archon needs at least one AI assistant. You can configure several and mix them in one workflow. This page covers what each provider needs installed, how it authenticates, and its
Which workflow features each provider supports is in the generated

Release binaries (quick install, Homebrew) ship without Claude, Codex and Pi. Add the ones you use:
archon provider add claude codex pi   # any subset

asks which to add and then sets up their authentication. An added provider must match the CLI version, so add it again after you upgrade Archon. Adding a provider connects Archon to the agent; it does not install the agent's own CLI. Your native configuration and login (

text.insert: Use Claude Code with a Claude Pro or Max subscription, an OAuth token, or an Anthropic API key.
Archon does not bundle Claude Code. Install it with Anthropic's native installer:

# macOS / Linux / WSL
curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash

# Windows (PowerShell)
irm https://claude.ai/install.ps1 | iex

Archon asks Claude Code for session-state events and finishes a node when the session goes idle after its final result. The CLI the bundled SDK ships emits them. If the process hangs instead, the node fails at the idle timeout, saying the provider never signalled that its turn settled.

Native credential checks request a sign-in refresh through app-server. If Codex reports no account, Archon rechecks once in a fresh process under the same deadline: another process may have saved a working login while the first retained a rejected refresh token. Pi caches the result of an API key stored as

for the life of the process, keyed by the command text. All Pi nodes in one Archon server share that cache. If the command returns a short-lived token, the server keeps sending it after it expires. Restart the server to run the command again, or use a longer-lived credential. Keys and headers from
commands are not cached this way.

An exception that escapes a detached extension callback, such as a timer or a watcher, fails the Pi node that loaded the extension instead of the Archon process. Archon routes it by the extension path in the stack. If several running Pi nodes loaded that extension, each fails with an error that says so. An escaped error that names no loaded extension still ends the process.

assistants:

    model: gpt-5-mini              # for example gpt-5, gpt-5-mini, claude-sonnet-4.5; unset passes auto
    modelReasoningEffort: medium   # any Archon effort, clamped to the SDK's low..max

    logLevel: error                # none, error, warning, info, debug or all
Copilot has no session-fork API. When Archon asks for a fork on retry, it starts a fresh session and posts a warning.

A run checks the credentials its AI nodes need before it creates isolation, and again before any node runs when execution starts or resumes. Vendors the run does not use are not checked, and a child workflow checks its own graph when it starts.
, a connected credential that cannot be read or is rejected blocks the run. Archon never falls back to another account.

, or with no connected credential, runs use the provider's native or environment account, and a missing login blocks launch. A host run checks that login before isolation; a container run checks it inside the container.
Claude checks account information in the target directory with each node's setting sources, without a model request. An
must exit successfully with a non-empty credential, unless an environment credential authenticates instead.
Providers that cannot check without a model session, including Copilot, OpenCode and Claude cloud backends, report "not checked" and may proceed.
A check that cannot decide (the vendor or the provider's runtime gave no answer, or the 60 s check timed out) does not block the run. The run starts and records a
event with the evidence, shown in the Web UI. A bad credential then fails the first AI node as
, without retry. A connected credential is refreshed again when execution starts, and blocks the run then if it still cannot be used.
A key that resolves is only usable; only a model request proves the vendor accepts it.
